newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Stamp fever engulfs Hongkong as empire fades.
newsitem.headline: Stamp fever engulfs Hongkong as empire fades.

text.p: Stamps tend to rise in value as the countries that issued them disappear or change political systems.
If you missed the chance to get the stamps of the Soviet Union and other former communist countries before they disintegrated, it may not be too late to cash in on Hong Kong.
Stamp collectors in Hong Kong have become crazed as Britain prepares to return the territory to China after more than 150 years of colonial rule.
The fad claimed a death when a 71-year-old philatelist collapsed and died of a heart attack in the stampede to buy the last stock of Queen Elizabeth stamps.
The British queen's face will disappear from Hong Kong mail forever on July 1, a day after the territory of 6.4 million people is handed back to China.

Thousands of stamp fanciers lined up for a day at post offices across the territory in February to pick up the "Year of the Ox" commemorative stamps, the last Lunar New Year issue to include a motif of the British crown.
"Our Lunar New Year stamps usually are the most popular, but I can't deny the fact that 1997 is contributing to some of the demand," said Aubrey Au, controller of posts.
The four-stamp set of colourful oxen is the 11th in a series of 12 issues celebrating the Chinese Lunar Year cycle.
Wong Ming-kit waited six hours at the General Post Office in Hong Kong's Central District for a chance to add the series to a collection he has been amassing for 30 of his 37 years.
"I'm buying them partly because they are the Lunar New Year stamps and partly because they have the crown," he said.
Au said 23 of Hong Kong's 125 post offices opened early to accommodate the rush.
Steven Chang, who has been collecting for decades, said his five-hour wait in line was worth it. "After I get the Year of the Ox, I will have 11 of the 12 signs," he said.
Sales of the final print of Hong Kong stamps bearing Queen Elizabeth's likeness and the first print of post-handover stamps featuring Hong Kong's skyline are hot items.
Many people collect stamps for their beauty and historical value, but in money-minded Hong Kong the prospect for profit also plays a key role.

The Hong Kong Post Office currently is under investigation after allegations that workers at its Shatin branch rigged the sale of special stamps to speculators. The market value of the ill-gotten stamps is about HK$500,000 ($64,100).
First-press issues of Year of the Ox stamps reportedly are selling at a 50 percent premium to their face value.

"There is a mixture of interests," Hong Kong Postmaster General Robert Footman said at Hong Kong's recent stamp exhibition. "Certainly the stamps have not lost value, but we are trying to build interest in the schools in stamp collecting as a hobby."

Hobbyists were clearly in evidence at the stamp show, which attracted tens of thousands of visitors with a showing of rare stamps, scores of international stamp exhibitors and, more important, the lure of inexpensive souvenirs.

On offer were cookie-box size replicas of the soon-to-be- scrapped British red mail boxes, stamps of Hong Kong at night, stamps of Hong Kong in the 19th century, stamps of Hong Kong that are really holograms and other memorabilia.
The mail boxes were hot items, and not because purchasers expect the tin toys to rocket in value.
"I bought them for my children," said one man as he hurried away from line.
The Intergovernmental Philatelic Society was doing a brisk business in "Action King" stamps featuring Kung Fu film star Jackie Chan at HK$100 ($12.91) a pop.

Across the room at the sprawling Hong Kong Convention Centre, people waited for a chance to shell out HK$300 ($38.74) for a 24-carat gold stamp featuring Hong Kong's Olympic windsurfing champion Lee Lai-shan, better known as San-san.

Pansy Ku, director of the Singapore gallery for Spink, a unit of British auctioneer Christies International, said collectibles have grown in value in Asia as an increasingly affluent population tries to buy back its cultural heritage.
"We see huge prices for Chinese ceramics and Indonesian paintings. Stamps and banknotes are in the same category because of the high prices and the enthusiasm," said Ku.
"This is more the case in Hong Kong than in Singapore. It might be the temperament of Hong Kong people. They never do anything half way," she said.
But people buying novelty stamps in hopes of big gains probably will be disappointed, Ku said. Gold-plated issues like the San-san stamp rarely surge in value.
"Stamps like that don't necessarily go up in value unless they are very rare. They really are only souvenirs," she said.
